questions.title: Distributed Tracing with Micrometer and Zipkin
questions.question: How do you implement distributed tracing in Spring Boot microservices?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Trace ID: unique per request across all services; Span ID: unit of work within one service**
- **Micrometer Tracing (Spring Boot 3+): replaces Sleuth**
- **Zipkin or Jaeger: trace visualization backends**
- **Propagation: trace context passed via HTTP headers (`traceparent` W3C standard)**
- **Sampling: don't trace 100% in production — performance cost**
- **MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context): include trace ID in log messages for correlation**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Distributed tracing answers the question: "For this user request that touched 5 services, where did it spend its time and where did it fail?" Each request gets a unique trace ID that propagates through all services via HTTP headers. Each service creates spans — one span per service involvement — and reports them to a centralized backend like Zipkin or Jaeger, which stitches them into a waterfall timeline.

In Spring Boot 3, this is done with Micrometer Tracing (which replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth). You add the dependency, configure a sampling rate and exporter, and trace propagation happens automatically — RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign clients all propagate the trace context without any code changes.

The critical operational insight: always include the trace ID in your log output via MDC. When a user reports an issue with a request ID, you can search logs across all services using that single trace ID and reconstruct exactly what happened.
